notes: A230 — Mobility & Stretching free-session pool. Separate from exercises.json by design: this catalog must NEVER be reachable by the climbing-session resolver. Schema follows exercises.json conventions where an equivalent exists (prescription_defaults, unilateral, equipment_required, fatigue_cost, stress_tags, recency_group). image is a filename under frontend/public/exercises/mobility/ (null = clean placeholder).

entries.name: Finger Flexor Stretch

prescription_defaults.notes: Per arm, 2 positions: set 1 palm-in (fingers toward you), set 2 palm-up (fingers away). Gentle pull-back on the fingers with the other hand, elbow straight.

entries.description: Extend your arm with the elbow straight and gently pull the fingers back with the other hand, first palm-in and then palm-up, to stretch the finger and wrist flexors along their full length. Keep the pull light and progressive — you are releasing climbing tension, not forcing range. Ease off immediately at any sharp pain in fingers, wrist or elbow. Based on Hörst's flexibility protocol (EX-STR-04).

entries.name: Finger Extensors Stretch

prescription_defaults.notes: Per arm. Elbow straight, flex the wrist and curl the fingers in, assist gently with the other hand over the back of the hand.

entries.description: With the elbow straight, flex your wrist down and curl the fingers in, using the other hand to add a gentle assist over the back of the hand — this targets the often-neglected finger and wrist extensors. It is a key epicondylitis-prevention stretch and is safe to do daily. Stop at any sharp pain, especially around the outside of the elbow. Based on Hörst's flexibility protocol (EX-STR-05).

entries.name: Pronator Pin & Stretch

prescription_defaults.notes: Per arm. Pin the pronator mass with the opposite thumb (~30s), then slowly pronate/supinate the forearm through its range while keeping the pressure on.

entries.description: Press the thumb of the opposite hand into the fleshy pronator mass just below the inside of the elbow, hold the pressure for about 30 seconds, then slowly rotate the forearm palm-up and palm-down while keeping the pin. This pin-and-stretch release melts pump-related tension that static stretching alone cannot reach. Never press directly on the epicondyle or on a tendon, and stop at any sharp or radiating pain. Based on Hörst's self-massage protocol (EX-SMR-04).

entries.name: Wrist Extensors Pin & Stretch

prescription_defaults.notes: Per arm. Pin the extensor mass below the outside of the elbow (~30s), then slowly make a fist and flex the wrist while keeping the pressure on.

entries.description: Pin the extensor muscle mass just below the outside of the elbow with the opposite thumb, hold for about 30 seconds, then slowly close the hand into a fist and flex the wrist down while keeping the pressure on. This targets the wrist extensors that stabilise every grip you take on the wall. Avoid pressing on the bony epicondyle itself, and stop at any sharp pain. Based on Hörst's self-massage protocol (EX-SMR-05).

entries.name: Finger Isolation Stretch

prescription_defaults.notes: Per finger, 2 rounds of 10s each. Gently extend one finger at a time back with the other hand, keeping the pull very light.

entries.description: Gently pull back one finger at a time with the other hand, holding a light stretch for about 10 seconds per finger, for two rounds. Working finger by finger reaches the individual flexor tendon units that a whole-hand stretch spreads too thinly. Keep the pressure conservative — fingers carry your climbing career — and stop at ANY pain, immediately. Based on Hörst's flexibility protocol (EX-STR-03).

entries.name: Anterior Shoulder/Chest/Biceps Stretch

prescription_defaults.notes: Interlace hands behind the back, lift the arms away from the body with the chest open. Shoulders back and down — never rolled forward.

entries.description: Interlace your hands behind your back, straighten the arms and lift them away from the body while opening the chest — this counteracts the rounded, pulled-forward posture climbing builds. Keep the shoulders drawn back and down throughout; never let them roll forward under the stretch. Ease off at any pinching in the front of the shoulder. Based on Hörst's flexibility protocol (EX-STR-08).

entries.name: Pectoral Release (ball)

prescription_defaults.notes: Per side. Pin a ball between your chest and a wall, search for tender trigger spots and hold each for 15–30s, breathing slowly.

entries.description: Trap a lacrosse or massage ball between your pec and a wall, then roll slowly until you find a tender trigger spot and park there for 15–30 seconds while breathing deeply. Releasing the pecs restores the shoulder-opening range that steep climbing steadily steals. Adjust the angle of your arm to reach different fibres. Stop at any sharp, radiating or nervy pain. Based on Hörst's self-massage protocol (EX-SMR-08).

entries.name: Doorway/Wall Chest Stretch

prescription_defaults.notes: Per side. Forearm on a doorframe or wall edge, elbow at shoulder height, step gently forward until you feel the chest open.

entries.description: Place your forearm against a doorframe or wall edge with the elbow at shoulder height, then step gently forward until you feel the chest and front of the shoulder open. Vary the elbow height slightly between sessions to bias different pec fibres. Keep the stretch gentle and stop at any pinching in the front of the shoulder. A staple in Lattice and Wirtz mobility routines for climbers.

entries.name: Posterior Shoulder Stretch

prescription_defaults.notes: Per side. Pull the arm across the chest with the elbow at ~90°, shoulder kept back — don't let it hunch forward.

entries.description: Pull one arm across your chest with the elbow bent to roughly 90 degrees, using the other arm to draw it in while keeping the shoulder pulled back rather than hunched forward. This targets the posterior deltoid and rotator cuff that stabilise every lock-off. Keep the shoulder blade set and ease off at any pinching deep in the joint. Based on Hörst's flexibility protocol (EX-STR-06).

entries.name: Rotator Cuff Stretch (towel)

prescription_defaults.notes: Per side. Towel/strap behind the back: top hand pulls up gently to draw the bottom arm higher. Light tension only.

entries.description: Hold a towel or strap behind your back with one hand over the shoulder and the other behind the lower back, then gently pull upward with the top hand to draw the bottom arm higher up the spine. Use light tension only — the rotator cuff responds to patience, not force. Ease off substantially if you have an impingement history, and stop at any sharp pain inside the shoulder. Based on Hörst's flexibility protocol (EX-STR-07).

entries.name: Sleeper Stretch

prescription_defaults.notes: Per side. Lie on the stretched side, arm at 90°, gently press the forearm toward the floor with the free hand. Contraindicated with anterior shoulder instability.

entries.description: Lie on your side with the bottom arm out at 90 degrees and the elbow bent, then use the free hand to gently press the forearm down toward the floor, stretching the posterior capsule into internal rotation. Go slowly — a few degrees of honest range beat a forced push. Do NOT do this stretch if you have anterior shoulder instability, and stop at any deep joint pain. Popularised in climbing rehab contexts by Lattice and Hooper's Beta.

entries.name: Thoracic/Upper-Back Foam Roll

prescription_defaults.notes: Roll the mid/upper back slowly, pausing 15–30s on tight spots. Support your head, keep the core lightly braced, don't roll the lower back.

entries.description: Lie on a foam roller placed across your mid-back, support your head with your hands, and roll slowly between the shoulder blades and mid-spine, pausing 15–30 seconds on any tight spot. Roll first, stretch second — releasing the tissue makes the stretches that follow far more productive. Keep the roller off the lower back and neck. Stop at any sharp or nervy pain. Based on Hörst's self-massage protocol (EX-SMR-01).

entries.name: Thread the Needle

prescription_defaults.notes: Per side. From all fours, slide one arm under the body until the shoulder rests on the floor; let the upper back rotate.

entries.description: From all fours, slide one arm palm-up underneath your body until the shoulder and ear rest on the floor, letting the upper back rotate open. This unwinds the thoracic rotation that steep climbing and desk time both lock up. Sink into the position with slow breaths rather than pushing. Stop at any pinching in the shoulder. Widely used in climbing mobility routines; pending literature validation at the next knowledge-base refresh.

entries.name: Cat-Cow (slow flow)

prescription_defaults.notes: Slow continuous flow, paced by your breath: inhale into extension (cow), exhale into flexion (cat). Stay in a neutral, pain-free range.

entries.description: On all fours, move slowly and continuously between arching the back up (cat) and letting it sink down with the chest open (cow), pacing each transition with a full breath. This is a flow, not a hold — keep moving gently for the whole timer, staying well within a pain-free range. Never force the end positions. Stop at any back pain. Described in Consuegra's mobility chapter (Ch. 8).

entries.name: Latissimus/Shoulder/Triceps Stretch

prescription_defaults.notes: Per side. Reach one arm overhead, bend the elbow behind the head, then lean sideways to run the stretch down into the lat.

entries.description: Reach one arm overhead, drop the hand behind your head, then use the other hand on the elbow and a sideways lean of the torso to run the stretch from the triceps down into the big pulling muscles of the lat. The sideways lean is what makes this a lat stretch rather than just a triceps one. Keep the ribs from flaring and stop at any shoulder pinching. Based on Hörst's flexibility protocol (EX-STR-09).

entries.name: Child's Pose (lat reach)

prescription_defaults.notes: Sit back on the heels, arms stretched far forward, chest sinking. Walk both hands to one side for a unilateral lat bias. Avoid with acute knee issues.

entries.description: Kneel, sit back toward your heels and walk the hands far forward until the chest sinks and the lats draw long. Walking both hands over to one side turns it into a deep unilateral lat stretch — do both sides if you take that option. Avoid this position with acute knee issues, and stop at any knee or shoulder pain. A recovery staple in Wirtz's routines for climbers.

entries.name: Passive Bar Hang (lat emphasis)

prescription_defaults.notes: Hang with soft scapular engagement (not fully slumped), feet on the floor or a box to regulate load. Avoid with impingement flare-up or pulley injury.

entries.description: Hang from a bar with a soft scapular engagement — not a dead slump — and let body weight traction the lats and spine, keeping the feet on the floor or a box to take out as much load as you need. Ease in gradually; the feet-assist is the intensity dial. Avoid entirely during an impingement flare-up or with any pulley injury, and stop at shoulder or finger pain. Pending literature validation at the next knowledge-base refresh.

entries.name: Piriformis Stretch

prescription_defaults.notes: Per side. Figure-4: ankle over the opposite knee, draw the legs toward the chest. Ease off at any knee, hip or low-back pain.

entries.description: Lie on your back, cross one ankle over the opposite knee in a figure-4, and draw the legs toward your chest until the stretch lands deep in the glute. The piriformis governs the hip turnout every drop-knee and high step depends on. Breathe into the hold and let it release gradually over the full minute. Ease off at any knee, hip or low-back pain. Based on Hörst's flexibility protocol (EX-STR-14).

entries.name: Pigeon Pose

prescription_defaults.notes: Per side. Front shin across the mat, back leg long, chest settling forward. Reduce depth at any knee discomfort.

entries.description: From all fours, bring one shin forward across the mat, extend the other leg long behind you, and let the chest settle toward the floor for a deep external-rotation stretch of the hip. This is one of the deepest holds in the pool — enter slowly and let gravity do the work over the full minute. Reduce depth immediately at any knee discomfort, and stop at sharp hip or knee pain. A core hold in Lattice and Wirtz flexibility work.

entries.name: Glute Max/Med Foam Roll

prescription_defaults.notes: Per side. Sit on the roller, cross the ankle over the knee and lean into the glute; park ~60s on the glute-med trigger spot on the outer hip.

entries.description: Sit on a foam roller, cross one ankle over the opposite knee and lean into the glute of the crossed side, rolling slowly until you find the tender spot — then park there for about a minute, breathing slowly. The glute-med trigger point on the outer hip is the money spot for climbers. Stop at any sharp, radiating or nervy pain down the leg. Based on Hörst's self-massage protocol (EX-SMR-02).

entries.name: Buttocks & Lower-Back Stretch

prescription_defaults.notes: Per side. Lying on your back, hug one knee to the chest while the other leg stays long on the floor.

entries.description: Lie on your back and hug one knee in toward your chest while the other leg stays long and relaxed on the floor, letting the glute and lower back release together. Keep the lower back heavy on the ground rather than curling up to meet the leg. Breathe slowly and deepen only as the tissue lets go. Stop at any low-back or hip pain. Based on Hörst's flexibility protocol (EX-STR-10).

entries.name: Adductor Stretch (legs up wall)

prescription_defaults.notes: Lie with the legs up the wall and let them slide apart under gravity; extend up to 120s as it releases. Socks reduce heel friction on the wall.

entries.description: Lie on your back with the legs straight up a wall, then let them slide apart under their own weight and give the adductors time — this deep gravity stretch can be extended up to two minutes as the tissue releases. Wearing socks reduces heel friction and lets the legs settle more smoothly. It's a long, intense hold: come out slowly by helping the legs together with your hands. Stop at any sharp groin or knee pain. Based on Hörst's flexibility protocol (EX-STR-12).

entries.name: Groin Stretch (butterfly)

prescription_defaults.notes: Soles of the feet together, sit tall, let the knees sink. Optional gravity phase: stay 1–2 min letting the legs settle without pushing.

entries.description: Sit tall with the soles of your feet together and let the knees sink toward the floor, holding the position while the groin gradually releases. An optional gravity phase of one to two minutes — no pushing, just settling — pays off for frogging and wide stemming positions. Press down through the sit bones rather than rounding the back. Stop at any sharp groin or knee pain. Based on Hörst's flexibility protocol (EX-STR-13).

entries.name: Seated Straddle (pancake)

prescription_defaults.notes: Sit tall, legs wide, hinge forward with a flat back. PNF option: press the legs into the floor 10–15s, relax, then deepen.

entries.description: Sit with the legs wide, grow tall through the spine, and hinge forward from the hips with a flat back — reaching with the chest, not the head. For the PNF option, press the legs down into the floor for 10–15 seconds, relax, and then sink a little deeper into the new range. Depth earned with a flat back transfers to the wall; a rounded slump does not. Stop at any groin or hamstring pain. From the Lattice MyFlex material.

entries.name: Hip Flexors & Quads (kneeling lunge)

prescription_defaults.notes: Per side. Kneeling lunge, tuck the pelvis and shift forward; keep the spine neutral or slightly extended.

entries.description: From a kneeling lunge, tuck the pelvis slightly and shift your weight forward until the stretch lands in the front of the rear hip and thigh. Keep the spine neutral or just slightly extended — arching the lower back fakes the range and wastes the hold. Tight hip flexors are what keep your hips off the wall on steep terrain. Stop at any knee or low-back pain. Based on Hörst's flexibility protocol (EX-STR-15).

entries.name: Hip Flexor / IT Band Foam Roll

prescription_defaults.notes: Per side. Roll slowly from the front of the hip down the outer thigh, up to 60s per side, pausing on tender spots.

entries.description: Lie face-down propped on your forearms with a foam roller under the front of one hip, and roll slowly from the hip flexor down along the outer thigh, pausing on tender spots for up to a minute per side. Keep the pressure tolerable — a slow melt beats a painful grind. Stop at any sharp, radiating or nervy pain. Based on Hörst's self-massage protocol (EX-SMR-03).

entries.name: Hamstring Stretch (supine, strap)

prescription_defaults.notes: Per side. On your back, strap around the foot, leg straight up; other leg long on the floor. PNF: press into the strap 6s, relax, deepen.

entries.description: Lie on your back with a strap or towel around one foot and take the straight leg up until the hamstring draws tight, keeping the other leg long on the floor. This is the pool's best PNF candidate: press the leg into the strap for about six seconds, relax, and take up the new range — an approach strongly supported in the stretching literature (Hindle 2012). Keep the pelvis heavy and the knee honest. Stop at any nervy pain down the leg. Based on Hörst's flexibility protocol (EX-STR-11).

entries.name: Deep Squat Hold

prescription_defaults.notes: Sit into a full deep squat, heels down, chest tall; use elbows inside the knees to open the hips. Put a block/book under the heels if ankle-limited.

entries.description: Sink into a full deep squat with the heels down and the chest tall, using the elbows inside the knees to gently open the hips — this one position trains hips, ankles and posterior chain together, and mirrors every resting position on the wall. If limited ankle mobility tips you backward, put a block or book under the heels. Stay relaxed and breathe for the whole minute. Stop at any knee or hip pain. A Lattice staple.

entries.name: Standing Forward Fold

prescription_defaults.notes: Hinge forward, knees soft, arms and neck fully relaxed. Bend the knees more if you have acute low-back issues.

entries.description: Hinge forward from the hips with soft knees and let the arms, head and neck hang completely relaxed, letting gravity lengthen the whole posterior chain. The relaxation is the technique — a tense fold stretches nothing. Bend the knees generously if you have acute low-back issues, and roll up slowly one vertebra at a time when done. Stop at any low-back pain or nervy sensation down the legs. From the Lattice flexibility material (§18).

entries.name: Calf Stretch (step)

prescription_defaults.notes: Per side. Ball of the foot on a step, heel sinking below it, knee straight — targets the gastrocnemius.

entries.description: Stand with the ball of one foot on a step or low block and let the heel sink below it with the knee straight, loading the big gastrocnemius muscle of the calf. Keep the movement into the stretch slow and controlled — no bouncing at the bottom. Calves that release well keep your heels down on slabby smears and long edging pitches. Stop at any Achilles or calf pain. Based on Hörst's flexibility protocol (EX-STR-16).

entries.name: Wall Soleus Stretch (bent knee)

prescription_defaults.notes: Per side. Facing a wall, back foot flat, drive that knee toward the wall with the heel down — bent knee shifts the stretch to the soleus.

entries.description: Face a wall with one foot back, keep that heel firmly down and bend the back knee forward toward the wall — bending the knee moves the stretch off the gastrocnemius and into the deeper soleus. The soleus is the muscle that lets your ankle close on high feet and rockovers, which makes this the highest-value calf stretch for climbers. Move in and out slowly. Stop at any Achilles or ankle pain. Described in Consuegra (D57).

entries.name: Kneeling Ankle Dorsiflexion Mobilization

prescription_defaults.notes: Per side. Half-kneeling, front foot flat: drive the knee out over the toes with the heel down, oscillating gently at end range.

entries.description: From half-kneeling with the front foot flat, drive that knee forward and slightly out over the toes while keeping the heel glued down, oscillating gently at the end of the range rather than holding rigidly still. This mobilizes the ankle dorsiflexion that high steps and deep drop-knees demand. Keep the oscillations small and smooth. Stop at any pinching at the front of the ankle. Pending literature validation at the next knowledge-base refresh.

entries.name: Seated Spinal Twist

prescription_defaults.notes: Per side. Seated, one leg crossed over: rotate toward the top leg with a tall spine, head level. Switch leg positions when you switch sides.

entries.description: Sit tall with one leg crossed over the other and rotate the torso toward the top leg, using the opposite elbow against the knee for gentle leverage while keeping the head level and the spine long. Rotation you own on the ground becomes cross-through reach and flagging stability on the wall. Remember to switch leg positions when you switch sides. Stop at any low-back pain. Based on Hörst's flexibility protocol (EX-STR-18).

entries.name: Supine Spinal Twist

prescription_defaults.notes: Per side. On your back, drop one bent knee across the body, shoulders heavy on the floor, gaze the other way. Relaxation emphasis.

entries.description: Lie on your back, draw one knee up and let it fall across your body toward the floor while both shoulders stay heavy on the ground and your gaze turns the opposite way. This is a relaxation twist — let breath and gravity do the work rather than pulling the knee down. It's an ideal way to close a session and downshift the nervous system. Stop at any low-back pain. A recovery staple in Wirtz's routines.

entries.name: Abdominal Stretch (cobra)

prescription_defaults.notes: Face down, press the chest up with the hips staying on the floor; elbows can stay bent to moderate depth.

entries.description: Lie face down and press the chest up with the arms while the hips stay grounded, opening the abdominals and the front line of the trunk that hours of body tension keep shortened. Keep the elbows bent as much as you need — height is not the goal, length in the front of the body is. Let the shoulders stay away from the ears. Stop at any low-back pain. Based on Hörst's flexibility protocol (EX-STR-17).
